query: Consider the following context: Melting properties are critical for designing novel materials, especially for discovering high-performance, high-melting refractory materials. Experimental measurements of these properties are extremely challenging due to their high melting temperatures. Complementary theoretical predictions are, therefore, indispensable. One of the most accurate approaches for this purpose is the ab initio free-energy approach based on density functional theory (DFT). However, it generally involves expensive thermodynamic integration using ab initio molecular dynamic simulations. The high computational cost makes high-throughput calculations infeasible. In that context, which method can be used for calculate its melting properties, including the melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change at the melting point, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Using machine‐learning-based interatomic potentials (MLIPs) to conduct molecular dynamics simulations with thermodynamic integration or coexistence methods will yield reliable predictions of melting temperature, fusion entropy, enthalpy, and volume change at the melting point in high‐melting refractory materials while dramatically reducing computational cost compared to full ab initio DFT approaches.
generation.material_initial_state: A refractory material, for example a high‐melting BCC-structured alloy used in applications requiring extreme temperature stability.
generation.intervention: Replace the expensive DFT free-energy thermodynamic integration method with MD simulations driven by MLIPs (trained on a representative DFT dataset) to calculate the free energy difference between solid and liquid phases.
generation.conditions: High-temperature MD simulations under periodic boundary conditions using a validated ML potential; simulations conducted using either the coexistence technique or thermodynamic integration to determine phase boundaries.
generation.structural_mediator: The ML potential accurately captures atomistic interactions, including anharmonic effects, thus mediating the accurate description of both solid and liquid phases.
generation.mechanism: MLIPs, trained on DFT data, emulate the accuracy of ab initio calculations but at a fraction of the computational cost, allowing high-throughput evaluation of phase free energies. This enables prediction of melting properties by comparing free energy curves of the two phases under comparable conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: It is predicted that the MLIP-based simulations will yield melting temperatures, fusion enthalpies and entropies, and volume changes at melting within an acceptable error margin (e.g., within ±10% of DFT predictions), making them suitable for high-throughput screening of refractory materials.
generation.baseline: Current ab initio free-energy approaches based on DFT are accurate but computationally prohibitive for high-throughput calculations.
generation.boundary: The method’s accuracy depends on the quality and representativeness of the training data for the ML potential; it may require additional validation when applied to novel refractory chemistries or when strong anharmonicity is present.
generation.uncertainty: There remains uncertainty regarding the exact error margins across diverse refractory systems and whether the ML potential can fully capture the necessary anharmonic and melting dynamics, particularly for systems outside its training set.

falsification_experiment.design: Develop an ML-based interatomic potential for a selected refractory high-entropy alloy using DFT-calculated training data. Perform melting property calculations (melting temperature, entropy and enthalpy of fusion, and volume change) using both the MLIP-based MD simulation (via coexistence or thermodynamic integration) and the conventional DFT free-energy method on the same alloy. Compare the results quantitatively.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the MLIP-based method yields property predictions that differ systematically from the full DFT results by more than an acceptable error margin (e.g., > ±10%), then the hypothesis that ML-based MD simulations can serve as an efficient and accurate alternative is falsified.
